You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis

Details: The failing test `testOverrideMeanWithMathClass` uses a `SummaryStatistics` instance and overrides the mean implementation with a new `Mean` object using `setMeanImpl(new Mean())`. The test then adds data values and asserts that the mean computed by the overridden mean implementation matches the manual evaluation of the `Mean` object on the same data.

From the code of `SummaryStatistics.setMeanImpl()`, before replacing the mean implementation, the method `checkEmpty()` is called, which throws an exception if the statistics object already contains values (`n > 0`). This ensures that the state of the object is empty when the implementation is changed.

The `getMean()` method delegates the mean calculation to `meanImpl.getResult()`, so replacing the mean implementation affects the future results.

The current bug report concerns a similar API approach with variance: invoking `setVarianceImpl(new Variance(...))` when the statistics object already has data causes `getStandardDeviation()` to produce NaN since `getStandardDeviation()` relies on the `getVariance()` method, which depends on the variance implementation. Since the setVarianceImpl also calls checkEmpty(), if it is called after values are added, it will throw, or if circumvented, it may cause inconsistent state leading to NaN in standard deviation.

Therefore, the root cause of the failure or issue appears to be that setting a new statistic implementation (mean, variance) after adding values leads to an inconsistent or empty state, as `checkEmpty()` prevents mutation otherwise. If the caller bypasses or the state changes improperly, the result of the statistics functions can become NaN due to lack of state or an uninitialized implementation.

Thus, the bug is caused by the invariant that statistic implementations may only be set on empty `SummaryStatistics` objects. The failing test, which sets the mean implementation before adding values, succeeds, but the current bug report shows that setting variance implementation after adding values leads to NaN in standard deviation.

Hence, the cause is the validation in `checkEmpty()` combined with state-dependent behavior of statistic implementations, leading to NaN results if violated.

No relevant recent bug reports were found to contradict or clarify this diagnosis.

Recommended fix: either enforce the empty state requirement strictly (throw exceptions) or provide mechanisms to reset or recompute statistics when changing implementations with data present.

This fully explains the failure in the test (which follows rules properly) and the bug report showing a related problem with variance and standard deviation.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
